FOR THESE REASONS, THE COURT
................................................................................. 18

[
1
]

The McGill University Health Centre (“
MUHC
”) has filed an Application to Introduce
Proceedings for an Authorization of Care (the “
Application
”). The MUHC asks the Superior
Court to order Ms. C. L. (“
C.
”)
[1]
to
undergo treatment. C. strongly contests the Application.

[
2
]

For the following reasons, the Court will grant
the Application in part. In doing so, it is mindful of C.’s strenuous
objections, for whom this order – according to her testimony – is worse than
remaining confined indefinitely on a psychiatric ward. Just before the close of
the hearing, C. asked: “Whose life is this anyway?” She also stated that she
“deserves a shot to live life on my own terms.” Respectfully, it is precisely
because the Court wishes C. to take control of her life and live it on her own
terms that it has made this difficult, but in its view necessary, decision
based on the evidence and the applicable law.

1.

Procedural Context

[
3
]

On February 7, 2023, the Court appointed Mr. D.
L. (“
Mr. L.
”), C.’s younger brother, as her “legal representative on a
provisional basis, for purposes of the exercise of her civil rights.”
[2]

[
4
]

On March 8, 2023, the Court ordered $25,000 be
advanced “to be used solely for the payment of the legal fees, disbursements,
and applicable taxes to be incurred for [C.] by her attorneys […].”
[3]

[
5
]

The Court rendered a similar order on April 14,
2023.
[4]

[
6
]

On June 26, 2023, the Court of Quebec ordered C.
“to submit to provisional confinement to undergo psychiatric assessment at the
MUHC or any other institution where she would be transferred in accordance with
the law for a period not exceeding four (4) days […].”
[5]

[
7
]

On June 30, 2023, the Court of Quebec ordered C.
“to submit to authorized confinement in an institution at the MUHC or any other
institution where she would be transferred in accordance with the law for a
period not exceeding 21 days […].”
[6]

[
8
]

On July 14, 2023, the Court ordered C., who was
then hospitalized at the MUHC, to “submit to a medical and psychosocial
examination to determine her capacity to exercise her civil rights and to
administer her property by the professionals at the [MUHC] or by any other
institution or professional designated to do so by the MUHC.”
[7]

[
9
]

On July 24, 2023, the Court of Quebec ordered C.
“to submit to authorized confinement in an institution at the MUHC or any other
institution where she would be transferred in accordance with the law for a
period not exceeding 30 days […].”
[8]

[
10
]

On August 22, 2023, the MUHC filed the
Application at issue in this case. It names C. as defendant and Mr. L. as an
impleaded party.

[
11
]

On August 29, 2023, the Court addressed matters
relating to C.’s representation.

[
12
]

On August 31, 2023, the Court acknowledged that a
sum would be paid from the patrimony of Mrs. M. A., C.’s mother, to retain
counsel on C.’s behalf. It designated Me Yohann Elbaz to represent C.’s
interests and set a hearing date for September 22, 2023.

[
13
]

On September 22, 2023, the Court rendered a
judgment postponing the hearing until October 19, 2023.

[
14
]

Despite a further verbal application for a
postponement (which was dismissed from the bench), the hearing was held for a
full day on October 19, 2023.

2.

Diagnosis and Care Plan

[
15
]

According to the testimony and medical report of
Dr. Warren Steiner, qualified by the Court as an expert in psychiatry, C. has
been suffering from an ongoing psychosis due to schizophrenia. According to Dr.
Steiner, psychosis is a disorder of brain function characterized by “positive”
symptoms (such as disorganized thinking, grandiose thoughts, hallucinations,
and delusions of persecution) and “negative” symptoms (such as mood swings,
inability to care for oneself, and lack of judgment and insight). In Dr.
Steiner’s opinion, “[w]ith this illness not being treated, [C.] will continue
to be in a psychotic state, and all of her life decisions will be driven by her
illness.”
[9]

[
16
]

Because C. has been hospitalized in a
psychiatric ward of the Montreal General Hospital (the “
MGH
”) for fours
months, allegedly suffers from acute positive and negative symptoms due to
psychosis, and refuses treatment, the MUHC asks the Court to render a care and
placement order consisting of:

Medical psychiatric, psychological, and psychosocial examinations;

Regular or intensive medical, psychiatric, and
psychosocial follow up with C.’s treating team when discharged from hospital;

The administration of long-acting intramuscular
and/oral antipsychotic medication for the treatment of schizophrenia, such as Paliperidone or Aripiprazole;

The administration of any adjunctive medications
required to counteract any possible side effects C. may experience;

The transfer and placement of C. in a structured
and supervised environment recommended by the MUHC Social Services; and

Adjustments and periodic
medical evaluations (the “
Care Plan
”).
[10]

[
17
]

The MUHC also asks that: (i) the Care Plan be
administered despite C.’s neglect or refusal for a period of 24 months;
[11]
(ii) C. be re-hospitalized for a period not exceeding 30 days
should her state of health so require;
[12]
and (iii) the Court’s care order “be executory notwithstanding any
appeal, after the five day delay to appeal provided by
Article 361
of the
Code
of Civil Procedure
[“
C.C.P.
”].”

3.

Evidence Adduced at the Hearing

[
18
]

At the hearing, the Court heard testimony from
four witnesses: (1) Dr. Steiner;

(2) Ms. Clarinda Daley, a Professional Social Worker working with C. at the
inpatient unit of the MGH, who was qualified as an expert in social work; (3) C.;
and

(4) Mr. L..

3.1

Dr.
Steiner’s Testimony

[
19
]

Dr. Steiner’s testimony (as supplemented by his
medical report) can be summarized as follows:

C. has a long history of mental illness going
back to 1997. She was in the Anxiety Disorders Program of the MUHC from
2013 to 2015 and treated with antipsychotic medication. The dosage of this
medication was reduced, and C. later dropped out of follow up.
[13]

In August of 2021, the manager of her apartment
building expressed strong concerns about C.’s behaviour, including her
belief that she was being persecuted by her family.
[14]

C. was admitted to the MGH in February of 2022
and seen by Dr. Steiner due to delusions of persecution and to aggressive
and disorganised behaviour. At that time, an application for protective
confinement (“garde en établissement”) was dismissed.
[15]

C. was brought by police to the Emergency Room
of the MGH seven months later in September 2022 due to unusual and erratic
behaviour, such as sleeping in the lobby, garage, and laundry room of her
apartment building. She was also harassing neighbours and building staff. C.
left the ER and fled Montreal.
[16]

For the next eight months, she lived as a
homeless person in Ontario as she believed her family was pursuing and
persecuting her. She frequented homeless shelters and lived in unhygienic
and dangerous conditions. C. was eventually arrested and hospitalized in
Kitchener, Ontario.
[17]

C. was transferred back to the MGH on June 22,
2023.
[18]

According to Dr. Steiner, C. is suffering from
an acute psychosis, a diagnosis confirmed by other senior psychiatrists
[19]
that has likely existed since February of 2022. Among other
things, she has extensive delusions of persecution.

Different disorders can cause psychosis. In C.’s
case, she suffers from late-onset schizophrenia. Because of the negative
symptoms associated with schizophrenia, individuals suffering from the
disease have a shorter life expectancy.

Although C. has been diagnosed and treated for obsessive
compulsive disorder (“
OCD
”) in the past, this does not explain her
current condition. C. believes she has OCD, but not psychosis or
schizophrenia or any other problem that would cause her to become
homeless. According to Dr. Steiner, any attempt to speak with C. about her
condition leads to a barrage of accusations against her family.

C. sees her father as a dangerous and abusive
man. However, Dr. Steiner does not think C.’s father raped or tried to
murder her and knows he did not try to pay off her psychiatrist. Dr.
Steiner does not think C.’s paranoid beliefs have any basis in fact.

Given her condition, C. cannot function outside
of hospital.

Because C.’s psychosis is untreated, her
condition continues to deteriorate. When he first saw her, she was wearing
dirty and urine-soaked clothes. She has ultimately agreed to shower three
times per week.

Dr. Steiner
has been C.’s physician for 2.5 months and sees her three times a week for
short visits, which can be explosive. During these consultations, C.
shouts at him and yells about psychiatric abuse. C. is abusive to nursing
staff and other patients and blocked off a common area of the psychiatric
ward. She also got into a verbal altercation with another patient that
could have become physically dangerous for her. The current situation is
not easy for C., nursing staff, and other patients.

C. has stated that she wants to be transferred
from the MUHC to a francophone hospital. Dr. Steiner has not objection to
this, provided she is able to find another psychiatrist.

C. has been in hospital for four months without
treatment, which is unheard of.

In Dr. Steiner’s opinion, there is no
alternative to the medical treatment provided for in the Care Plan. If C.
follows this Care Plan, she can be expected, in the midterm, to develop
better insight and judgment, become less abusive, feel less persecuted,
and be less at risk of being physically assaulted.

The medication contemplated in the Care Plan is
second-generation medication that is a dramatic improvement over first-generation
medication. It involves much less movement disorders. There can be side
effects, however, including metabolic syndrome, associated weight gain,
and increased cholesterol. C. would therefore be monitored via regular
blood tests.

The Care Plan would enable C. to be stabilized
and out off hospital within three or four weeks.

Therapy would need to be conducted for cognitive
behaviour post-discharge, nursing care, and social care. According to Dr.
Steiner, C.’s social integration is very important. She will continue to
be a risk to herself and lack judgment. It will take time for C. to
recover and obtain insight. For this reason, it is realistic for the Care
Plan to last 24 months
.

Although the possibility of C. being able to
leave the psychiatric ward has been discussed, her psychosis and
aggressiveness makes this unadvisable. As Dr. Steiner acknowledges, “This
is inhumane. This is unfair to her.” Were C. to begin to be treated
pursuant to the Care Plan, she would be able to leave the ward five times
a day for 30-minute periods, provided she was behaviourally appropriate.

[
20
]

While C.’s testimony regarding Dr. Steiner was extremely critical, the Court
is convinced, based on the evidence, that he is a conscientious, good faith professional who wants to
assist C. by treating the illness he and his colleagues have diagnosed.

3.2

C.’s
Testimony

[
21
]

C.’s testimony can be summarized as follows:

C.’s father generated wealth over a period of
decades, notably through a shopping centre project.
[20]
This is the money she is now being excluded from.

C. comes from an uncaring family. She was
sexually abused by her father at an early age. Ever since, he has become
an “arch enemy” and there is no possibility of a reconciliation with him.
[21]

According to C., her maternal grandmother
suffered from OCD, she herself developed OCD at about the same age, and
she was prescribed Anafranil by a psychiatrist and psychoanalyst. Although
her symptoms cleared up as a result, she gained 40 pounds. Eventually, she
went off the medication.

C. moved out of her home and into an apartment
at 28 with the (reluctant) help of her father and the “guy who broke my
heart.”

At 30, C. moved to Toronto, where her brother B.
and her sister-in-law L. were living.

At 42, C. returned to Town A from Toronto and
was set up in an apartment by her mother. She was supported from a trust
fund created for her and her two brothers. Although C. said she enjoyed a
good lifestyle, she was nevertheless under her father’s control.

C.’s OCD returned and she began to consult with
Dr. Sam Stein, who put her back on Anafranil. This caused C. to gain
weight once again. According to C., Dr. Stein seemed to believe there was
a diagnosis other than just OCD, one possibly connected to another illness
or damage from abuse. She was also prescribed an antipsychotic drug. At no
point was she diagnosed with schizophrenia.

According to C., “antipsychotic drugs have
ruined lives.” She derived very little benefit from her medication, which
she took for five years, and suffered from side-effects such as weight
gain and bad skin. She “didn’t need these problems in her life.”

In 2004, C. left for the Greek islands and was
considered a missing person for 10 days. When she returned to Town A, she
booked herself into the [Hotel A]. She was later confined in the
Sacré-Coeur Hospital.

Afterwards, C. began living in a Town A
apartment whose lease was guaranteed by her mother and received funding
from a trust. During this time, C. “never missed a rent payment” and
“became a huge shopper.”

At one point, C. found herself at the MGH and
was assigned to Dr. Pierre Bleau at the Allan Memorial Hospital. He
prescribed antipsychotic medication. C. said she had a falling out with
Dr. Bleau and wanted to be on the lowest dosage possible. Dr. Bleau did
reduce the dosage and C. decided to take herself off all the drugs.
According to her, the antipsychotic medication she was taking changed her
personality by making her more subdued and less combative.

According to C., she was sent to the Emergency Room
of the MGH “under false pretences.” Dr. Bleau saw her and “signed the
papers for her to stay.” She remained in hospital for four days and was
“freed” by a judge.

She met Dr. Steiner at this time. According to C.,
she took an immediate dislike to Dr. Steiner, who was “patriarchal,” did
not allow her to elaborate on her background, and “wanted to keep her in
his hands.” Dr. Steiner is “unfair and insensitive.” She has never spoken
with Dr. Steiner for more than five minutes and he does not know her.

C. testified Dr. Steiner has lied about her. She
is not a danger to others, nothing happened to her when she was homeless,
and she never resisted arrest.

C. says her father has given millions of dollars
to MUHC hospitals and has instructed them to keep her confined.

Her family engaged the mafia at some point and
there is no way for her doctors to know that this is not the case.

C. insists she does not agree with her diagnosis
of acute psychosis and schizophrenia. She testified that “she’s
complicated and can’t be diagnosed in 15 minutes.”

According to C., “she completely disagrees with
the treatment plan.”

As things currently stand, C. is “incarcerated
in a horrible place,” “wants to escape her family,” and “just can’t take
it anymore.”

[
22
]

In support of her contestation, C. has filed
three exhibits:

➢

Exhibit D-1
: A
handwritten letter in which C. explains, among other things, her dislike of,
and unwillingness to be seen by, Dr. Steiner.

➢

EXHIBIT D-2
: A
handwritten letter in which C. objects to Mr. L. acting as her mother’s
curator.

➢

Exhibit D-3
: An
article dated November 16, 2022 concerning a $15.3 million gift made by the [Foundation
A]¸ to McGill University in order to create the [Centre A].

[
23
]

The foregoing summary does not capture every
aspect of C.’s testimony, which covered many different periods of her life. The
Court notes C. is a highly intelligent, vivacious, and communicative person who
made it a point to explain her experiences and wishes to the Court.

3.3

Ms.
Daley’s Testimony

[
24
]

Ms. Daley’s testimony (as supplemented by her
psychosocial assessment)
[22]
can be summarized as follows:

Her role consists of working with psychiatrists
and staff at the MGH, following patients, and providing them with support.

Ms. Daley first met C. on February 24, 2022, and
resumed contact on June 23, 2023, when C. was transferred to the MGH from
the Grand River Hospital in Kitchener, Ontario.
[23]

She meets with C. two times per week and assists
her with her finances, including budgeting. According to Ms. Daley, C.
receives $50 on Monday and $50 on Friday from Mr. L.. Although C. accepts
this money from Mr. L., she has no connection with him. She also refuses
to accept new clothing provided by her brother. According to Ms. Daley, C.
believes Mr. L. is controlled by their father. C. also takes umbrage at
the fact that Mr. L. was granted tutorship of their mother.

As C. refuses treatment, Ms. Daley testified
that her role is limited to assisting C. with finances, listening to her,
and liaising on her behalf with the MGH team.

Because C. had no financing for housing between
September 2022 and June 2023, she was evicted from her apartment
[24]
and ended up in Ontario, where she was homeless and
frequenting homeless shelters. According to Ms. Daley, C. was assaulted at
one of these shelters.

C. told Ms. Daley that she intends to get out of
Town A as soon as possible to escape her family.

C. has had poor hygiene since her admission.

Although smart and logical, C. has no insight or
judgment.
[25]

C. would like to live in an apartment. Should
she get the treatment she needs pursuant to the Care Plan, Ms. Daley would
assist C. in finding an apartment with outpatient follow up (“
Option A
”)
or, should that not be possible, a supervised group home or intermediate
centre (“
Option B
”). The decision as to whether to proceed with
Option A or Option B will depend on the assessment of C.’s needs and
functioning.
[26]

If C. is untreated, Ms. Daley does not think she
could live safely in an apartment on her own. For example, C. must be
prompted incessantly to wash herself and her clothes. There is also a risk
that C. would flee Quebec.

During her four months at the MGH, C. has
received no visits from friends.

The psychiatric ward where C. is located is
secured, so that she is never able to leave its confines.

C. refuses to accept treatment and is verbally
abusive to staff and other patients.
[27]

3.4

Mr. L.’s
Testimony

[
25
]

Mr. L.’s testimony can be summarized as follows:

He was appointed tutor for his and C.’s mother
in 2021, as she suffers from Alzheimer’s disease.

C. disappeared in 2004 and he was able to track
her, with the assistance of police, to the [Hotel A] in Town A, where she
was secluded and hostile. Although C. agreed to go to hospital by
ambulance, she refused to be admitted to the Jewish General Hospital because
of her father’s association with that institution. She was then
transferred to the Royal Victoria Hospital and, ultimately, the
Sacré-Coeur Hospital. Mr. L. described C. as “manic, aggressive, and
ranting” at the time.

Following this hospitalization, C. moved into an
apartment on Drummond Street and was financially maintained via a trust
fund established by her father, Mr. Irving L., for the benefit of his
three children. This trust was later converted into a corporation.

C. was able to manage her affairs until the
Christmas season of 2019, when Mr. L. was told she had not been paying her
rent for four months. Mr. L. paid the rent owing and developed a
relationship with the manager of C.’s apartment building, who informed him
later on of “alarming things.” More specifically, C. was asking other
tenants for money, spending hours in the lobby, selling goods in the
lobby, sleeping in other parts of the building, simultaneously renting
another furnished unit, and returning to the building bloody and
dishevelled. Moreover, C. would not allow social workers or employees of
the Local Community Service Centre into her apartment.

The last payment made to C. from the corporation
created by her father was in August or September of 2022. Since that time,
all money provided to her has been withdrawn from her mother’s patrimony
at Mr. L.’s instruction.

When Mr. L. was able to visit C.’s apartment to
vacate its contents (following her eviction), it looked like a warehouse.
The apartment was so cluttered it was impossible to move about. There were
unclean dishes in the kitchen, and everything appeared to be in disarray.
[28]

Because Mr. L. thought it “looked like a car
crash was coming,” he brought proceedings for protective supervision and
was appointed provisional tutor. Although a safeguard order was issued, C.
did not comply with it.

C. went missing in the fall of 2022 and was
traced to Ontario in the first weeks of October. From October 2022 to May
2023,
[29]
she went from shelter to shelter and lived on the street.
During this time, she was assaulted and concussed on at least one
occasion. Mr. L. hired a private investigator to locate C. and track her
movements.

C. was picked up by police in Kitchener,
Ontario. Mr. L. drove to Ontario, where he spent five days. C. was
admitted to the Grand River Hospital and administered an intramuscular
injection following a “Code White” incident.

When asked why he has done what he has for his
sister, Mr. L. stated it was important for him to fulfil his duties as
tutor to his mother.

Mr. L. testified that he comes from a
dysfunctional family but said he does not believe his father sexually
abused C.. Moreover, Mr. L.
completely rejects the notion that his father is in any way connected with
the mafia.

Mr. L. further testified he believes C. needs
medication and wants her to be comfortable going into old age. If she does
not follow the Care Plan, he fears she will die on the streets of some
other city. According to Mr. L., “this is her last chance at salvation.”

He likes to think back on C. when she was an
older sister to him.

[
26
]

Despite C.’s strongly expressed resistance to
Mr. L.,
[30]
the Court is of the view that his testimony was compelling and
truthful. The Court concludes, based on the evidence, that Mr. L. has been a
dutiful tutor, son, and brother, and that he has acted with a view to C.’s best
interests. It also recognizes that Mr. L.’s dedication has come at a
significant personal cost. As he testified, he feels as though his life is
“dripping away in the process.”

4.

Applicable Principles and Case Law

[
27
]

As stated by the Court of Appeal in
M.B.
c.

Centre hospitalier Pierre-Le Gardeur
, respect for the autonomy,
inviolability, and integrity of the person is a fundamental value of Quebec law
in matters of care.
[31]
In effect, this value is enshrined in both the
Charter of Human
Rights and Freedoms
,
[32]
which enjoys a quasi-constitutional status, and the
Civil Code
of Québec
(“
C.C.Q.
”).
[33]
More recently, the Court of Appeal observed that compelling a
person to take or be administered medication against his wishes is to infringe
his fundamental rights.
[34]
Moreover, care can only be imposed on an exceptional basis and must
be treated accordingly – that is, restrictively.
[35]

[
28
]

These principles are clearly explained and
invoked in C.’s written arguments.
[36]

5.

Article 16 C.C.Q.

[
29
]

In deciding whether to order the Care Plan, the
Court must undertake the analysis developed by the Court of Appeal in
F.D.

c.

Centre universitaire de santé McGill (Hôpital Royal-Victoria)
.
[37]
In the first place, it is necessary to consider the criteria of

article 16

C.c.Q.
:

16.

The authorization of the court is necessary where the person who may give
consent to care required by the state of health of a minor or a person of full
age who is incapable of giving his consent is prevented from doing so or,
without justification, refuses to do so;
it is also necessary where a person
of full age who is incapable of giving his consent categorically refuses to
receive care, except in the case of hygienic care or emergency.

The authorization of the court is
necessary, furthermore, to submit a minor 14 years of age or over to care which
he refuses, except in the case of emergency if his life is in danger or his
integrity threatened, in which case the consent of the person having parental
authority or the tutor is sufficient.

[Underlining
added]

[
30
]

As noted by the Court of Appeal, a meticulous
analysis is required for any authorization of care order made pursuant to

article 16
C.C.Q. for a person of full age who is allegedly incapable of giving
consent. The Court can only move on to the next step of the test if the one
prior has been met, it being understood that the burden of proof rests squarely
on the applicant.
[38]

5.1

Is C.
Incapable of Giving Consent?

[
31
]

In the Court’s respectful view, C. is not able
to give consent. Dr. Steiner’s testimony and his medical report are convincing
evidence that C. is in a state of acute psychosis caused by schizophrenia.

[
32
]

Although C. admits she suffers from OCD, Dr.
Steiner’s testimony convinces the Court that her current symptoms – as
described by Dr. Steiner, Ms. Daley, and Mr. L. – are not those associated with
OCD (i.e. delusional paranoid thoughts, lack of judgment and insight,
aggressive behaviour, dangerous behaviour, poor hygiene, slovenliness, etc.).

[
33
]

The fact C. was not diagnosed with schizophrenia
earlier in her life, or in the context of her consultation with other medical
professionals, is not evidence that she cannot therefore be suffering from the
disease now. As Dr. Steiner testified, schizophrenia can occur later in life.

[
34
]

The Court also accepts Dr. Steiner’s conclusions
that C. has likely been in an acute psychotic state since at least February of
2022, that her condition will only deteriorate if she is not given medical
treatment, and that her condition cannot be treated without the use of antipsychotic
medication.

5.2

Does
C. Categorically Refuse to Receive Care?

[
35
]

With respect to the refusal to receive care, C.
made it very clear in her testimony that she rejects the diagnosis of acute
psychosis caused by schizophrenia. While she admits to having OCD and possibly
another illness rooted in childhood abuse, she states she is a complex person,
and that Dr. Steiner has not made a good faith attempt to truly understand her
condition. According to C., she “completely disagrees with the treatment plan.”
[39]
The Court recognizes this as a categorical refusal.

[
36
]

In addition to C.’s rejection of her diagnosis,
she also pointed to the side-effects associated with her use of antipsychotic
medication in the past. This medication produced physical effects, namely
significant weight gain and bad skin, and modified her personality by making
her “more subdued and less combative.”
[40]
The Court takes these concerns very seriously. According to Dr.
Steiner, however, the Care Plan contemplates the use of second-generation
antipsychotic medication that does not have the significant side effects of its
first-generation predecessors. The Court also acknowledges that C.’s treating
physicians and the MGH staff will closely monitor her condition to avoid or
mitigate any undesirable side effects.

6.

Article 12 C.C.Q.

[
37
]

As the Court has concluded C. is incapable of
giving consent and categorically refuses to receive care, it must pursue its
analysis by considering, in the second place, the criteria of article 12
C.C.Q.:

12.

A person who gives his consent to or refuses care for another person is bound
to act in the sole interest of that person, complying, as far as possible, with
any wishes the latter may have expressed.

If he gives his consent, he
shall ensure that the care is beneficial notwithstanding the gravity and
permanence of certain of its effects, that it is advisable in the circumstances
and that the risks incurred are not disproportionate to the anticipated
benefit.

[Underlining added]

[
38
]

As the Court of Appeal states in
F.D.

c.

Centre universitaire de santé McGill (Hôpital Royal-
Victoria
)
, regardless
of whether an application for an authorization of care is contested, judges
must consider each of the relevant factors.
[41]

They cannot delegate this responsibility, which the legislature has conferred
to them rather than medical professionals.
[42]

6.1

Is
the Care Required and Described with Sufficient Precision?

[
39
]

The Court concludes the Care Plan outlined in
Dr. Steiner’s medical report, reproduced in the Application, and explained by
Dr. Steiner in his testimony is required – most notably insofar as the
administration and types of antipsychotic medication are concerned – and sufficiently
precise. The assessment approach, the medication that will be used, its method
of administration, and the monitoring of side-effects, among other things, are
clearly substantiated by the expert evidence and well articulated. The Care
Plan is neither so general as to be ambiguous nor so highly detailed as to be
inaccessible to C. and the Court.

6.2

Are
the Risks Incurred Disproportionate to the Anticipated Benefit?

[
40
]

As noted above, the Court is mindful of C.’s
concerns regarding the side-effects associated with the administration of
antipsychotic medication. It also accepts C.’s testimony in this regard. For
this reason, the Court takes act of Dr. Steiner’s assurances that: (i) the
antipsychotic medication to be used is different from that previously
administered to C.; and (ii) any side effects will be closely monitored and
mitigated.

[
41
]

That said, the Court is convinced the risks
incurred are greatly outweighed by the anticipated benefits. Without minimizing
the possibility or seriousness of potential side effects, the current situation
is untenable. C. has been living in a psychiatric ward for four months. She is
unable to leave the premises and has only done so to attend the hearing. C.
testified she is “incarcerated in a horrible place.” Similarly, Dr. Steiner
testified that this situation is “unheard of,” “inhumane,” and “unfair to C..”
On this point at least, C. and Dr. Steiner agree. The Court also agrees. In its
view, the status quo is unacceptable.

[
42
]

Based on a preponderance of the evidence, the
Court concludes that the Care Plan is the only way to put an end to this
prolonged confinement by treating C.’s acute psychosis, diminishing its
positive and negative effects, and ensuring she can transition out of hospital
and into either an apartment (Option A) or a supervised group home or
intermediate centre (Option B). The Court is convinced this will give C. the
control over her life and future she so passionately – and rightly – desires.
In short, the Care Plan is C.’s “best shot to live life on [her] own terms.”

[
43
]

As Dr. Steiner and Ms. Daley testified,
treatment that does not involve medication cannot address C.’s illness and
would not enable her to leave hospital and reassert her independence. The Court
accepts this testimony.

6.3

How
Long Should the Order Last?

[
44
]

Given the length of her psychosis (over 1.5
years) and the amount of time reasonably needed to treat her symptoms, the
Application proposes the Care Plan be administered for a 24-month period. Based
on the testimony of Dr. Steiner – according to whom it will take at least two
years for C. to regain her judgment and insight – the Court considers this
period to be reasonable in the circumstances. Given C.’s strenuous opposition
to the Care Plan and her subsidiary submission that the Care Plan only be in
effect for one year, the Court will exercise its discretion to reduce the
proposed duration of the Care Plan to 18 months and reserve the MUHC’s right to
seek an extension. This way, the length of the Care Plan will precisely match
the likely duration of C.’s acute psychosis.

6.4

Other
than the Care Plan and its Duration, Are Any Other Conclusions Sought?

[
45
]

There are two additional conclusions that merit
attention. The first is the one providing the Court’s care order be executory
notwithstanding any appeal, after the five-day delay to appeal provided for by

article 361

C.C.P.
The Court understands C. strongly objects to this conclusion
given its impingement on her fundamental rights. Nevertheless, the Court is of
the respectful view, based on the evidence, that her circumstances are dire and
that the Care Plan must be implemented as quickly as possible. As mentioned
above, C. has already been confined to the psychiatric ward of the MGH for four
months. This inhumane form of prolonged hospitalization must come to an end.
The several weeks needed for an appeal will only aggravate conditions that are
already unacceptable.

[
46
]

Finally, C., the MUHC, and Mr. L. are open to C.
being transferred from the MGH to a French-language hospital that is not part
of the same university network. Indeed, C. has made it clear she does not like
or trust Dr. Steiner.
[43]
As Dr. Steiner testified, however, it would first be necessary for C.
to find a psychiatrist at a French-language institution. Her counsel has
helpfully agreed to assist her with this process and will be compensated via
Mr. L. in his capacity as tutor to Mrs. A.. The Court believes this transfer
may help to allay some of C.’s concerns and facilitate the healing process. Any
such transfer will not put an end to or modify the Care Plan in any material
respect unless the Court orders otherwise.

7.

RECOGNITION OF COUNSEL

[
47
]

Finally, the Court wishes to recognize the
invaluable assistance provided by all counsel in this case, as well as the
quality of their submissions.
